title: A Hidden Depth
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. reflects on Ann Hollingsworth's book about Fred Rogers, whose seemingly simplistic program rested on rigorous study of child development. He connects this to Peps Mccrae's argument that the better someone's teaching is, the simpler it looks to an outsider, a pattern he saw at Parker Core Knowledge school in Colorado. He admits the idea is a little annoying given how hard expert practice is to build, but finds it also intoxicating. The way to spot an expert, he says, is by impact rather than appearance, echoing Mccrae's framing of teacher expertise around influence on what students think, do and achieve. Rogers's 1969 Senate testimony shows hidden depth transforming a skeptical senator in six minutes. Stuart's practical conclusion is to seek expertise and understanding, to see students and their world, and to do this work with like-minded colleagues.
points: Expert teaching often looks simple to outsiders because the depth of understanding behind it is invisible.
Expertise is best judged by its impact on what students think, do and achieve, not by how the work looks.
Fred Rogers's apparent simplicity rested on deep knowledge of children, himself and the obstacles to healthy development.
Teachers today face an engagement bombardment far more perfected than the one Rogers criticized, which makes depth matter more.
The practical response is to seek expertise and understanding and to pursue it alongside like-minded colleagues.
